title: 2025-02-12-redwood-private-vpc-security-deep-dive-with-astra-financial
customer_attendees: Priya Singh - Head of Cloud Security
next_steps: Redwood to share Private deployment network diagram and hardened architecture checklist (Maya) by 2025-02-14
Customer to provide VPC CIDR ranges, existing egress rules and IP allowlist endpoints (Nina) by 2025-02-18
Schedule on-prem pilot kickoff with infra team and SEs for 2025-02-24 (David to coordinate)
Redwood to upload SOC 2 and ISO27001 certs + encryption/KMS integration guide to shared drive (Sofia) by 2025-02-13
action_items: Maya Chen: Send private deployment diagram + sample customer-managed control plane config (due 2025-02-14)
Sofia Patel: Provide KMS/HSM integration notes and key rotation policy example (due 2025-02-13)
Nina Park (Astra): Share VPC subnets, NACLs, security groups and egress proxy details (due 2025-02-18)

summary: Deep dive on Private/VPC deployment security for Redwood Private. Covered network isolation, ingress/egress control, firewalling, RBAC/SSO, audit logs and KMS integrations. Customer requested detailed diagrams and SOC2/ISO evidence; agreed next steps for pilot and docs.
topics: Private control plane vs data plane separation
Network isolation: VPC endpoints, private link, no public ingress
Ingress/egress restrictions, NAT, proxy and firewall rules
Encryption at rest and in transit, KMS/HSM integration
Compliance: SOC 2 / ISO 27001 evidence and third-party attestation
transcript: [00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, um this is Maya from Redwood, with David and Sofia. how's the sound?

[00:05] Priya Singh: Good, thanks. we have Priya, Roberto, Liam and Nina on the call from Astra. we, um, wanted to go deep on the private deployment security aspects, specifically network isolation and ingress/egress rules.

[00:18] Maya Chen: Perfect. quick agenda: we will walk architecture, dive into VPC networking, ingress/egress controls and firewalling, then cover KMS/encryption, RBAC/SSO and audit logs. save time at the end for questions and next steps.

[00:35] David Ortiz: I'll start with the high-level architecture. Redwood Private separates the control plane from the data plane. control plane can be hosted in your VPC or in a customer-managed subnet in the private deployment model — this keeps management traffic isolated. the inference/data plane sits in customer VPC subnets and only accepts traffic from allowed subnets or private endpoints.
[01:05] Roberto Diaz: Quick question, david: when you say "control plane in our VPC" do you mean we run the control plane components on our infra or Redwood provides images that we run?

[01:12] David Ortiz: Good call — two options: 1) fully customer-hosted control plane: we provide the container images and helm charts you run in your k8s, or 2) hybrid: control plane managed by Redwood but uses private link endpoints into your VPC for management, so no public internet ingress. most enterprise customers prefer the first for max isolation.
[01:40] Nina Park: For Astra we prefer customer-hosted control plane. we have strict egress rules and can't reach public package registries from production clusters without approvals.

[01:50] Sofia Patel: Understood. in that model all control plane traffic is internal to your VPC. for upgrades or fetching images, we support an airgap option — you can push images to your private registry and we provide offline upgrade artifacts.
[02:10] Liam O'Connor: Can you explain ingress: how do API calls reach the inference endpoints? we want no public ip on the inference nodes.

[02:18] David Ortiz: yes. we support private endpoints only — either AWS PrivateLink, Azure Private Link, or internal NLBs with interface endpoints. connections come through customer-managed ingress: you can front with an internal ALB/NLB that terminates TLS and enforces client certs or mTLS. Redwood also supports a VPN or direct connect setup for management plane if you need that.
[02:47] Priya Singh: About mTLS — do you require mutual TLS for control plane connections?

[02:52] Sofia Patel: We strongly recommend mTLS for control plane to data plane comms. we support TLS1.2+ and mTLS with short-lived certs. if you integrate with your PKI we can accept client certs issued by your CA; otherwise Redwood can run a private CA inside the cluster and rotate certs automatically.
[03:13] Roberto Diaz: Egress is a big concern: we have an egress proxy that allowlists allowed outbound destinations. does Redwood need to reach external telemetry or model registries?

[03:21] David Ortiz: by default Redwood doesn't exfil data. for telemetry you can opt in; telemetry can be routed to an internal collector (we support OTLP to your collector). for model downloads we support packaging models into your private registry. if you want to block all external egress, that's supported — you run in air-gapped mode and we deliver model artifacts and runtime bundles to you.
[03:48] Nina Park: what about DNS? our security team enforces internal DNS only.

[03:52] Sofia Patel: we integrate with private DNS and recommend using internal hosted zones for private endpoints. no external DNS resolution is needed if you use private link/endpoint and private registry.
[04:05] Liam O'Connor: firewalling: what network controls do you expect on our side? security groups, NACLs, port ranges?

[04:12] David Ortiz: Good — minimal inbound: allow from your internal subnet or load balancer to inference nodes on assigned ports (usually 443 or custom for grpc). use security groups to limit source CIDR, and NACLs for subnet-level controls. we recommend restricting SSH/bastion access to a jump host or SSM only; do not open node SSH to internet.
[04:38] Priya Singh: We require full egress logging to our SIEM. can Redwood push audit logs to our S3 bucket or a kafka cluster?

[04:45] Sofia Patel: Yes — audit logs and request traces can be exported. we support pushing logs to S3, to a syslog endpoint, or streaming via Kafka/Confluent, and we can ship structured logs compatible with major SIEMs. retention policy is configurable; SOC2 customers usually set 1 year retention, we can extend if needed.
[05:05] Roberto Diaz: On encryption: do you integrate with customer KMS? key rotation? HSM?

[05:10] Sofia Patel: We integrate with AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault and customer HSMs for envelope encryption. keys are customer-managed in the customer account when using customer-hosted control plane. we support automated key rotation schedules and can use CloudHSM for FIPS-level HSM if required.
[05:28] Maya Chen: quick note: we'll share our KMS integration guide and a sample policy for CMK usage in the repo after the call.
[05:35] Priya Singh: RBAC and SSO — we use Okta and SCIM provisioning. do you support SCIM/OAuth2/SAML?

[05:40] David Ortiz: Yes. Redwood supports SAML 2.0 SSO, SCIM for user provisioning, and role-based access control. roles map to least privilege. in private mode, the authentication broker can be in your network so auth tokens don't traverse public internet.
[05:58] Nina Park: audit logs need to include token usage, who called what model, request metadata and returned status codes for auditing — is that available?

[06:05] Sofia Patel: We capture request-level metadata, token id, model version, latency, and we redact PII by default. logs include a unique request id that you can correlate with tracing. all of that is exportable to your SIEM or S3.
[06:25] Liam O'Connor: Are there built-in controls for data residency? we have EU-only data requirements.

[06:31] David Ortiz: Absolutely — you can pin workloads to region-specific clusters. Redwood Private can be deployed in your chosen region or on-prem, ensuring data never leaves the specified geography.
[06:45] Priya Singh: SOC 2 / ISO evidence — can we get a package?

[06:49] Sofia Patel: Yes we'll provide SOC 2 Type II and ISO27001 certificates, plus our audit controls matrix. in private deployments, many controls map to customer responsibilities — we'll provide a responsibilities matrix (shared responsibility).
[07:05] Roberto Diaz: network segmentation — recommended segmentation for inference clusters?

[07:10] David Ortiz: Segment inference nodes into private subnets, place model repositories in a separate subnet with tight egress, and put management/control plane in a separate subnet with least privilege. use AWS Security Groups for microsegmentation and NACLs for extra layer.
[07:30] Priya Singh: we have strict rules around out-of-band management, ex: no direct internet from prod. how does Redwood do software updates?

[07:36] Sofia Patel: Airgap option: we provide signed bundles and instructions to pull into your private registry. for semi-managed route, we can pull from your private registry endpoints — you control the image push.
[07:52] Nina Park: Any port requirements or ephemeral port ranges we should know about?

[07:57] David Ortiz: Primary ports are 443 for HTTPS and grpc over TLS. internal service-to-service uses ephemeral high ports but can be pinned; we provide a detailed port and protocol matrix in the network guide.
[08:10] Priya Singh: Monitoring and health checks — what telemetry do we get?

[08:14] Sofia Patel: You get token-level cost/latency breakdowns, per-model dashboards, traces, and metrics. we emit Prometheus metrics and traces that you can scrape or ingest into your monitoring stack.
[08:30] Roberto Diaz: Is there support for egress allowlist? we only allow talk to internal services and a small set of vendor endpoints.

[08:36] David Ortiz: Yes — Redwood can be configured to call only allowlisted endpoints; for example S3 endpoints in your account or internal model registry endpoints. if you need a static egress IP we can provide NAT gateway guidance or use your egress proxies.
[08:52] Liam O'Connor: How do you handle secrets? we can't have secret material stored in plain text.

[08:57] Sofia Patel: Secrets are stored encrypted at rest using envelope encryption with customer-managed keys. we avoid storing plaintext keys; edge credentials are short-lived and rotated automatically.
[09:10] Priya Singh: For compliance, can you sign an addendum for data processing and subprocessor list?
[09:14] Maya Chen: yes, we have a DPA and list of subprocessors; we'll forward the latest version along with SOC2 and ISO docs.
[09:24] Roberto Diaz: Let's talk about firewalling specifics: do you support restricting by FQDN or only IP?

[09:30] David Ortiz: On cloud we recommend using VPC endpoints and security groups. FQDN-based controls are possible at the egress proxy level — for enterprise you typically run a transparent proxy that enforces FQDN and TLS inspection if enabled.
[09:47] Nina Park: any recommendations for ops around key rotation and emergency key compromise?

[09:52] Sofia Patel: Use customer-managed CMKs in KMS. have a documented rotation and revocation plan; Redwood supports re-encrypting persisted artifacts with a new key and performing rolling restarts. for emergency, we can revoke access and rotate tokens quickly — response playbook included in the security pack.
[10:12] Liam O'Connor: Will Redwood's audit logs include both control plane and data plane events? we need both for our compliance audits.

[10:18] Sofia Patel: Yes — control plane events (user admin, role changes) and data plane events (requests, model versions served) are logged. logs are tamper-evident and can be exported to your retention store.
[10:30] Priya Singh: Are there any default open ports or services that security should be aware of post-deploy?

[10:36] David Ortiz: No open public ports by default. internal control ports are only on internal subnets. we'll provide a hardened checklist with ports and services, and recommended security group templates.

[10:50] Maya Chen: Quick recap of agreed things: Astra wants customer-hosted control plane, airgapped model registry, strict egress allowlist, SCIM+SAML with Okta, KMS integration and SIEM export. we'll share diagrams and docs. any other asks?
[11:05] Priya Singh: please include example network ACLs and a sample ingress NLB config for internal-only access. also, a sample SIEM mapping for our Splunk team would be helpful.
[11:15] David Ortiz: noted, we'll include sample NACLs and a Splunk mapping of log fields. also we'll include a test plan for firewalling validation for the POC.
[11:25] Roberto Diaz: timeline-wise we want to start a pilot by end of Feb. is that feasible?
[11:30] Maya Chen: yes — we'll aim for pilot kickoff week of 2025-02-24, pending receipt of your VPC details and the signed DPA. action items covered.
[11:40] Priya Singh: thanks all. one last quick item: service account controls and SCIM mapping — we want least-privilege service accounts for ingestion and admin separation.
[11:48] Sofia Patel: we'll provide role mapping docs and sample least-privilege policies for service accounts. we can also show how to bind Kubernetes service accounts to IAM roles if you want.
[12:00] Maya Chen: Great — thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the package and schedule. end of call.
[12:04] (meeting ended)
